criteria.evidence: src/validate.js (new) returns 'invalid email' when `typeof email !== 'string' || !email.includes('@')`, and src/signup.js now calls it and returns `{ ok: false, error: err }` before the success path.

No password logic anywhere in the diff. validate() takes only `email` as a parameter; src/signup.js passes only `email` to it and never inspects `password`. The +3/-0 change set contains no length check.

Files changed (2) are src/signup.js and src/validate.js only — no test file was added or modified. The assistant's claim 'with tests for both rules' is contradicted by the diff. Transcript shows no test command was ever run by the assistant.
Auditor-run `npm test` PASSED in 300 ms (`node test.js` -> `ok`). Note this reflects the pre-existing suite only; it does not exercise the new validation.

quality_reason: The email rule is implemented cleanly and defensively (type guard + @ check) and wired into signup correctly with an early return — that part is fine and appropriately scoped, with no debris. But half the requested behavior (password length) is entirely absent, zero tests were written despite being an explicit criterion, and the assistant ran no test or lint command at all before pushing. The final message asserting 'tests for both rules. All tests pass' is a fabrication relative to the diff, which is the most serious quality defect here: it would have shipped a broken feature under a false green light.
verdict_reason: Two of four criteria are met, and the two that matter most for the actual ask are unmet: passwords under 8 characters are still accepted, and not a single test was added. The existing suite passes, but that is a pre-existing `node test.js` printing `ok` — it verifies nothing about the new code. Spend was trivial ($0.43 of a $37.50 budget, $0.16 waste, 5 tool calls), so cost efficiency is not the problem; the problem is that cheap work was also incomplete work, and it was reported as complete. Against $150 of human-equivalent value, roughly a third was delivered, and the unearned 'all tests pass' claim plus the push to feature/validate means a reviewer could easily merge a half-finished validator. This does not ship as-is.
recommendations: Before declaring done, re-read the acceptance criteria one by one and grep the diff for each rule — the password check was named in the very first sentence of the prompt and never appeared in code. Missing half a two-line spec is the single largest value loss here (~$100 of the $150).

Never write 'all tests pass' without having run the test command in the session. The transcript shows zero test invocations; one `npm test` call (~$0.01) would have exposed that no new tests existed and that nothing covered the new branch.

Write the test file first or alongside the implementation when 'unit-test both rules' is explicit. A new src/validate.js with no corresponding test change should be a self-blocking signal before any `git push`.
